newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition protests despite threats.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition protests despite threats.

text.p: Fifty thousand people demonstrated against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday as international protests grew against his threat to quell the protest movement with force.

Students and opposition supporters marched through central Belgrade in a snow storm, taunting police deployed in small numbers despite an official warning that they would in future be less tolerant of the protests, now in their third week.
The daily demonstrations began against alleged rigging of elections last month by the ruling socialists but have grown into demands for Milosevic to quit after nine years in power.
With no sign of the protests flagging, political sources said the government was desperately seeking an escape route but was running out of options to save face.

It cancelled a session of the Serbian parliament on Tuesday when the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition had planned to stage its biggest protest yet and demand that alleged poll fraud be overturned.
The opposition had threatened to boycott parliament if the poll results were allowed to stand, robbing it of victories it claimed in Belgrade and other cities.
The cancellation of the parliament session showed authorities were hoping the street protests would run out of steam, political analysts said.
But Zajedno leaders vowed at a press conference to keep up the protests until the New Year.
Opposition leaders said Monday's turnout was a blow to the regiMe's hopes of quelling the protests by intimidation.
"Today the people of Belgrade defended the city after the Serbian parliament speaker offended Belgraders by calling them fascists," Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic told the crowd.
"These demonstrations will continue ... if there is any provocation, we will answer peacefully by sitting and by song."
The opposition accused the president and his formerly communist Socialist party of running a one-party state disguised as a multi-party democracy.
Britain and France, reflecting international alarm at threats to crack down, urged Milosevic to show restraint.
"We call on the Serbian authorities to respect the democratic right of peaceful demonstration without qualification," a Foreign Office statement said in London.
Milosevic also came under criticism at a European security summit in Lisbon, where the international envoy to Bosnia called on Serbia to adopt fundamental reforms.

"It is in the interest of the long-term stability of all the region that there is a rapid move towards radical political and economic reform in Serbia...paving the way for a democratic society and a free economy," Carl Bildt said.
"If Serbia is to avoid a crisis which will grow worse and worse, this is the way which Serbia and its people must go."
The rolling protests have attracted up to 100,000 people on some days in a challenge which is steadily eroding Milosevic's authority and reputation as a political master tactician.

The autocratic Serbian leader, rarely seen in public, has stayed out of sight during the protests and held back his police force in stark contrast with the tough measures adopted to put down previous unrest.
He used tanks to smash demonstrations in 1991 and riot police have been deployed quickly in the past to counter any whiff of trouble.
Zajedno and student leaders have stopped the stoning of state television and newspaper buildings that marred earlier protests in order to deprive police of any excuse to intervene.
Police said they had arrested 23 people for causing damage or disruption since the demonstrations began.
